steps.text: Gargamelle was a bubble chamber at CERN designed to detect neutrinos. In July 1973 its collaboration presented the first direct evidence of the weak neutral current, a process that required a neutral particle to carry the weak force.
steps.title: Hunting for weak neutral currents

claims.covers: leaving hadrons but no charged lepton
claims.quote: A beautiful hadronic neutral current event, where the interaction of the neutrino coming from the left produces three secondary particles, all clearly identifiable as hadrons, as they interact with other nuclei in the liquid. There is no charged lepton (muon or electron).

claims.quote: In both cases the neutrino enters invisibly, as usual, interacts and then moves on, again invisibly.

steps.text: In a hadronic neutral-current event the neutrino enters invisibly, interacts and moves on, again invisibly, leaving hadrons but no charged lepton. By March 1973 there were as many as 166 hadronic candidates and one single-electron event, and the two papers were published on 3 September 1973.
steps.title: What a neutral current looks like

claims.covers: CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron was used as a proton-antiproton collider from 1981
UA1 searched for traces of W and Z particles in its collisions
UA2's main aim was to study the W and Z bosons

steps.text: CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron was used as a proton-antiproton collider from 1981. UA1 searched for traces of W and Z particles in its collisions, and UA2's main aim was to study the W and Z bosons.
steps.title: A collider to make the W and Z

claims.covers: On 20 January 1983 UA1 announced six candidate W events
on 22 January UA2 announced four
UA1's events had isolated electrons of large transverse energy with associated missing energy
the signature of a particle of mass about 80 GeV/c²

steps.text: On 20 January 1983 UA1 announced six candidate W events, and on 22 January UA2 announced four. UA1's events had isolated electrons of large transverse energy with associated missing energy, and the signature of a particle of mass about 80 GeV/c².
steps.title: The W boson, January 1983

claims.covers: On 1 June 1983 CERN formally announced the discovery of the Z boson
UA1 reported four electron-positron pairs and one muon pair at about 95 GeV/c²
UA2 measured the Z mass as 91.9 GeV/c²

question.answer: In energy units the Z mass is 91.9 GeV, and one collision had 540 GeV in total. 91.9 ÷ 540 × 100 ≈ 17, so a Z at rest takes about 17% of that collision's energy.

question.prompt: UA1's W paper reports collisions at a total energy of 540 GeV, and UA2 measured the Z mass as 91.9 GeV/c². What fraction of a 540 GeV collision's energy is the Z mass?

steps.text: On 1 June 1983 CERN formally announced the discovery of the Z boson. UA1 reported four electron-positron pairs and one muon pair at about 95 GeV/c², and UA2 measured the Z mass as 91.9 GeV/c².
steps.title: The Z boson, June 1983

question.answer: ALEPH found N = 3.27 ± 0.30. The gap to N = 4 is 4 − 3.27 = 0.73, and 0.73 ÷ 0.30 ≈ 2.4 standard deviations. ALEPH's abstract says its result rules out the possibility of a fourth type of light neutrino at 98% CL.

question.prompt: ALEPH's measurement of the number of light neutrino species was N = 3.27 ± 0.30. How many standard deviations is N = 4 from that result?

steps.text: LEP's initial energy was chosen to be around 91 GeV so that Z bosons could be produced. A final combination of the LEP and SLC results found the number of light neutrino species to be 2.9840 ± 0.0082.
steps.title: Counting neutrinos with the Z

summary: From the 1973 hunt for weak neutral currents in a bubble chamber to the discovery of the W and Z in proton-antiproton collisions in 1983, and what the Z then taught LEP.
